entry.title: Who is bonded to whom?
entry.content:
My thesis follows what happens when the neighbors at an electrode change. Acetone and methylamine push Cu capacitance in opposite directions; about 13 ppm Cu remains in solution at −0.75 V versus RHE; and about 1 ppm Pb opens a much more effective route to reductive amination on Ag. At a ligand-confined Ag interface, partially desolvated Cs⁺ also makes closer contact with activated CO₂. Across three parts, I follow the same question: who is bonded to whom, and what becomes possible when those partners change?

In this post

  1. The electrode comes with company
  2. Three stops at the interface
  3. The calculations have different jobs
  4. Reach it, keep it, restore it
  5. A few distinctions worth keeping

The electrode comes with company

I can label an electrode Cu or Ag in a methods section. That label is useful, but it leaves out a lot of the chemistry happening right beside the metal. Water points in different directions. Reactants bind, exchange protons, and rearrange their neighbors. A metal atom can acquire enough new partners to leave the electrode altogether. The material on the invoice is only the beginning of the story.

My PhD work started from specific puzzles in aqueous electrochemistry. Why would two organic reactants change capacitance in opposite directions? Why would a reducing electrode lose metal? Why would a tiny amount of another element make a large difference to product yield? A later collaboration on CO₂ reduction brought in a different puzzle: what changes when a cation gives up some of its water?

I use coordination broadly here. It includes metal–ligand contacts, hydration, hydrogen bonding, and the metallic neighbors that hold a surface atom in place. These interactions have different physics. Following how they change gives me a useful way to connect the projects without pretending they all run on the same equation.

Three stops at the interface

The series follows a chemical progression: first the environment changes, then the electrode can change, then those changes in partners can open a reaction route.

Part 1 · Capacitance

Capacitance before reduction. Acetone raises Cu double-layer capacitance and methylamine lowers it. Both molecules are more polarizable than water on their own, so I had to look at the assembled interface.

Part 2 · Dissolution

When the cathode dissolves. Amines stabilize Cu as it trades metallic neighbors for nitrogen ligands. A cathodic potential helps retain Cu, but the solution chemistry still gets a vote.

Part 3 · Reactivity: Pb + Cs in CO2RR

Borrowed hydrogen and a nearly bare cation. Pb and Bi hydrides offer candidate hydrogen shuttles in amination. In a separate CO₂-reduction system, less hydrated Cs⁺ develops a closer, chemically specific adsorbate contact.

The final part deliberately puts two different reactions side by side. Pb and Bi change composition as they transfer hydrogen; Cs changes its local hydration and interaction with CO₂. Their connection is a change in coordination that creates a reactive configuration. I keep the experimental systems separate throughout.

The calculations have different jobs

My contribution across these studies was computational chemistry, alongside experiments that supplied the puzzles and tested the interpretations. For the Cs collaboration, I contributed to the electronic-structure and interfacial modeling; experimental collaborators performed the synthesis, electrochemistry, and spectroscopy.

I used a hierarchy of models because each question needs different detail. Explicit water resolves local organization. Molecular dynamics supplies configurations to inspect. Continuum solvent represents the surroundings without placing every molecule. Calculations at a common electrode potential let states exchange electrons with the same reservoir. Reaction-path calculations address hydrogen-transfer barriers.

More atoms are useful when they resolve something that could change the answer. For water response, I need molecular orientation. For Cu loss, I need kinks and ligands. For a hydride, I need the hydrogen donor and its transition state. For Cs, I need to vary hydration explicitly.

A detailed picture can still leave out the quantity I most want. A frozen water configuration can have a well-defined electronic response while its probability in the real liquid remains unknown. An optimized hydride can have an accessible transfer pathway while its steady-state concentration remains unknown. Keeping those gaps visible makes the calculation more useful.

Reach it, keep it, restore it

When I put the studies together, three practical questions kept appearing. Can the relevant configuration be reached? Can its essential species remain available long enough to do something useful? Can they be restored afterward?

Cu dissolution shows why reaching a new coordination environment can be bad news for the electrode. An amine helps a Cu atom leave its metallic surroundings and become a soluble complex. The hydride studies explore another possible fate for a mobile metal species: transfer hydrogen to the substrate, return to the electrode, and regenerate. Detachment is a branching point; what follows decides whether it is material loss or part of a productive cycle.

The Cs system supplies a different arrangement. A ligand-confined interface can retain the cation near the adsorbate while water coordination decreases. Losing water makes room for a closer contact. The useful change happens without requiring a metal-containing molecule to shuttle into solution.

I find this more helpful than asking for the strongest possible adsorption or the largest possible capacitance. A useful reactive configuration needs to be accessible, survive its competition, and fit into the rest of the chemistry. Strong binding can help one requirement and obstruct another.

A few distinctions worth keeping

The numbers in this series answer different questions, and I try to keep their job descriptions attached.

Response and population

Capacitance tells me how charge responds to potential. Several structures can give the same response trend. It cannot uniquely tell me how often each structure occurs.

Intermediate and barrier

An uphill intermediate carries an energetic cost. A transition state sets an activation barrier. An energy profile containing only intermediates does not supply a dissolution rate.

A step and a cycle

An accessible hydrogen-transfer step matters only if its donor forms, reaches the substrate, survives side reactions, and regenerates. A low barrier alone does not predict product yield.

Those distinctions come from the synthesis in my thesis, rather than from a wish to add caveats to every sentence. They help locate the next useful experiment or calculation. Measure populations, find the missing transition state, track the mobile metal, account for the water reservoir: each addresses a particular missing link.

The through-line is simple enough to keep in mind while the chemistry gets busier. Before assigning activity to a material, I want to know its neighbors under the conditions of the reaction. Part 1 starts with water, two solutes, and a capacitance trend that refused to follow the obvious explanation.
entry.summary: Part 0, Overview: three stops through my UCLA PhD thesis, from water and capacitance to Cu dissolution, molecular hydrogen shuttles, and Cs-assisted CO2 activation

entry.title: Borrowed hydrogen and a nearly bare cation

link.title: Borrowed hydrogen and a nearly bare cation

entry.content:
About 1 ppm Pb takes reductive amination on Ag from almost no amine to yields above 60%. My calculated preferred imine-hydrogenation barriers are 0.39 eV for PbH₄ in solution and about 0.47 eV for PbH₂ on Ag, versus above approximately 0.9 eV for the examined direct Ag routes. In a separate CO₂-reduction collaboration, reducing Cs hydration from five waters to one shortens its CO₂-oxygen contact from about 3.51 to 2.83 Å. Both stories turn on changing coordination, with donor regeneration and hydration-state populations still essential to the full explanation.

In this post

  1. A tiny impurity with a large effect
  2. Build a hydrogen donor
  3. A shuttle has to make the return trip
  4. Try another p-block passenger
  5. Give Cs a little less water
  6. Partial covalent means looking at the electrons
  7. A productive configuration needs a whole setting
~1 ppm Pbstrong experimental promotion of Ag amination
0.39 / 0.47 eVpreferred solution / surface Pb-assisted barriers
3.51 → 2.83 ÅCs–O contact, five- to one-water models, approximately

A tiny impurity with a large effect

Ag was a poor amination catalyst in a Pb-free cell. Add approximately 1 ppm Pb and amine yields exceeded 60%. That is a lot of catalytic influence from an ingredient that might otherwise be filed under impurities.

Part 2 showed how coordination can move metal into solution. Here I follow another possible consequence of metal mobility: a species that carries hydrogen to the substrate. The reaction is still acetone reductive amination. The CO₂ system comes later, as a separate example of coordination creating reactivity.

The experimental controls made the nominal Ag composition an incomplete explanation. A fresh membrane in an Ag–Pb cell gave approximately 29% amine yield; repeated use with a Pb anode raised it to approximately 64% by the fourth use. Elemental analysis found ppm quantities of Pb in the cathode compartment. Repeated membrane use in a Pb-free cell with a Pt anode did not reproduce that activation, while deliberate Pb addition restored high yields.

The protocols also matter. The galvanostatic series gave approximately 63% at 1 ppm Pb; the potentiostatic comparison at −2.94 V versus RHE gave approximately 61%. I keep those as separate comparisons. Rinsing an active Ag electrode and transferring it into Pb-free electrolyte dropped the reported yield from 61% to 1.1%. That argues against persistent activation surviving the transfer, while leaving room for a short-lived surface species under bias.

Build a hydrogen donor

I compared several possible hydrogen sources: H on Ag, water-mediated proton-coupled electron transfer, a surface Pb hydride, and a molecular Pb hydride in nearby solution.

At −2 V versus RHE, the calculated thermodynamics favor high H coverage on Ag(111). My starting model therefore carries 16 surface H atoms in a (4 × 4) cell. That specifies the environment in which the pathways are evaluated; it does not establish the exact H distribution on a real polycrystalline electrode.

Initial transfer from Ag to Pb has a calculated barrier of 0.68 eV. The next step to PbH₂ is approximately 0.51 eV, or approximately 0.48 eV with surface H replenishment. Direct water-mediated formation of the early hydrides has barriers above 1 eV in the examined structures. Early hydrides favor H pointing toward Ag, making the metal-side supply geometrically helpful.

Once PbH₂ forms, further addition through surface transfer or water-mediated steps can have barriers below approximately 0.5 eV. PbH₂ remains strongly associated with Ag in the tested structures, whereas PbH₄ has unfavorable adsorption free energy at −2 V and can enter solution. Changing the hydrogen count changes where the species can do chemistry.

For solution PbH₄, the preferred N-first imine hydrogenation has an effective barrier of 0.39 eV; its first step is 0.22 eV. Surface PbH₂ gives approximately 0.47 eV for the preferred N-first sequence. The examined direct Ag alternatives exceed approximately 0.9 eV at −2 V. The strongest comparison is the lower-barrier route opened by Pb. The 0.08 eV separation between the preferred Pb routes is too small to identify their dominant steady-state contribution.

A shuttle has to make the return trip

The solution proposal is a PbH₄/PbH₂ shuttle. Ag generates the hydrogen-rich species, PbH₄ leaves and supplies two H atoms to the imine, and PbH₂ returns for regeneration. Surface-bound PbH₂ offers an alternative route in which hydrogen transfer stays at Ag.

A favorable transfer barrier only gets the proposal partway home. Pb hydrides can react with water and release H₂; the reported side-reaction barriers are approximately 0.5–0.8 eV. Even with a lower preferred imine barrier, competition depends on encounter rates and activities. Water is abundant, and local imine availability depends on condensation and transport.

Electrochemical flow-cell measurements coupled to ICP-MS support a mobile Pb inventory. They do not directly identify PbH₄ in the working aqueous cell. Likewise, the nearly potential-independent amine yields over the reported −1.34 to −3.34 V window are compatible with a chemical solution step once donor generation is sufficient, but do not prove it is rate determining.

A hydride shuttle needs donor formation, survival, substrate encounter, and return. My calculations make Pb-mediated hydrogen transfer plausible and lower-barrier than the examined Ag routes. They leave the balance between surface and solution cycles open.

Try another p-block passenger

The next collaboration asked whether the mechanism could help select a different mediator. Experimental collaborators screened p-block additives, and I calculated hydrogen transfer for AsH₃, H₂Se, InH₃, SnH₄, SbH₃, H₂Te, TlH₃, PbH₄, and BiH₃.

These are the molecular models, not a census of aqueous species. The sixth-period TlH₃, PbH₄, and BiH₃ candidates give favorable product-forming landscapes in the comparison; the lighter candidates have less favorable intermediates or products. That is a result for this substrate and model family, rather than a periodic-table rule.

For BiH₃, the article reports a lower barrier of 0.29 eV for N-first hydrogenation and 0.56 eV for C-first. Transfer of two H atoms leaves BiH. The proposed return route brings BiH to Ag, regenerates BiH₃ through surface chemistry, and releases the donor again. This parallels the Pb proposal without assuming identical transport, adsorption, or hydrolysis.

At 1 ppm additive, reported amine yields were approximately 54.3% for Tl and 36.9% for Bi, against approximately 60.8% for the matched Pb reference; lighter tested elements gave approximately 1–3%. Increasing Bi to 6 ppm raised yield to approximately 59.7%, with no further benefit at 7 ppm. Similar yields at different inventories do not imply identical turnover frequencies.

Deep dive: why transfer energetics cannot rank the full mediators

A transition state must be referenced to its preceding intermediate, particularly if that intermediate lies well below the initial reactants. The comparison also needs donor formation and regeneration. In the Bi concentration series, yield rises while turnover number normalized to total added Bi falls, and reported carbon balances are roughly 70–75%. None of those measurements determines the fraction present as active BiH₃. At 6 ppm Bi and 25 °C, Pt and Ni gave yields below 10%, emphasizing that the electrode still matters for generating the proposed molecular donor.

Give Cs a little less water

The CO₂ collaboration starts from a different problem. At a ligand-confined Ag interface, how does water deficiency change what Cs⁺ can do for a CO₂-derived adsorbate? I contributed to the electronic-structure and interfacial calculations, alongside experimental synthesis, electrochemistry, and spectroscopy.

The catalyst is a nanoparticle-ordered ligand interlayer, or NOLI. Conditioning tetradecylphosphonic-acid-capped Ag nanoparticles detaches ligands that remain near aggregated particles. That environment contains water and ions, but differs from bulk electrolyte. The question is whether partial loss of hydration allows a closer, chemically specific Cs–O contact.

I compared seven constructed states, from remote six-water Cs to progressively less hydrated configurations near Ag(111). The remote reference leaves CO₂ nearly linear at 179.9°, with an average Cs–O separation of approximately 4.56 Å. Moving the six-water environment closer already bends CO₂ to approximately 171.0°.

Across the five- to one-water near-surface models, Cs–O distance falls from approximately 3.51 to 2.83 Å, and CO₂–Ag distance from approximately 2.82 to 2.19 Å. The corresponding Cs–O ICOHP values are approximately −0.11, −0.14, −0.18, −0.19, and −0.20 eV. Less hydration accompanies closer approach and a larger net bonding contribution within this model family.

The title’s nearly bare cation is still hydrated: even the least hydrated state retains one explicit water. Partial desolvation is the mechanism being tested.

Partial covalent means looking at the electrons

A shorter distance alone does not establish a bond type. I examined orbital overlap, differential charge density, electron localization, Bader charges, and crystal orbital Hamilton populations. Together, they support a partial covalent contribution alongside the substantial electrostatic interaction.

Cs⁺ remains an alkali-metal cation. Partial covalent character describes chemically specific electronic interaction in the Cs–O contact, without assigning an integer bond order or removing its ionic character.

Reference crystals help interpret the diagnostics. CsI, CsHCO₃, and Cs₂CO₃ contain the same element with different anion environments. For selected short contacts, average ICOHP is approximately −0.170 eV in Cs₂CO₃ and −0.177 eV in CsHCO₃. A more negative cumulative value in a larger contact network does not mean every individual bond is stronger. Contact count, unit-cell choice, and distance cutoff enter that sum.

The interfacial hydration comparison needs another kind of bookkeeping. CO₂ adsorption referenced to each prepared hydration state measures affinity conditional on that state. To predict populations, I must also pay the cost of preparing different water counts from a common reservoir, including water chemical potential. Favorable adsorption in the one-water model does not establish that one-water Cs is abundant.

Spectroscopy constrains the interpretation too. The published assignment is a partially reduced, activated CO₂-derived intermediate; its notation does not require a charge partition to place exactly one electron on it. Its vibrational signal precedes sustained CO production. The Cs M-edge series was collected after return to open circuit because faradaic current overwhelmed detection under bias, so it probes a relaxing post-polarization interface. Stabilization, population under bias, and turnover remain distinct questions.

A productive configuration needs a whole setting

Pb and Bi offer candidate mobile hydrogen donors. Cs offers a closer adsorbate contact while remaining near a confined Ag interface. In both cases, changing partners creates a chemically different possibility; realizing it depends on the rest of the setting.

That closes the thread from water response to Cu loss to reactivity. I need to know which configurations can be reached, whether their essential species remain available, and how the cycle restores them. Those questions keep the useful molecular explanation connected to the measured experiment.

Where this was published

This post follows thesis Chapters 5 and 6. The Pb impurity experiments appeared in Angewandte Chemie International Edition (2024); the Pb mechanism calculations in Catalysis Science & Technology 16, 4090–4102 (2026); and the p-block screen and Bi study in Angewandte Chemie International Edition (2026). I performed the Pb reaction-path and p-block hydrogen-transfer calculations. The desolvated-cation study appeared in Nature Catalysis 9, 1009–1022 (2026); my contribution there was computational.
entry.summary: Part 3, Reactivity: Pb + Cs in CO2RR: hydride shuttles offer a route to amination, while partial Cs desolvation strengthens contact with activated CO2 in a separate Ag system

entry.title: When the cathode dissolves
entry.content:
An 18-minute cooling interval left the subsequent amine yield at 3.9 ± 0.2%; protective cathodic polarization during cooling raised it to 30 ± 2%, and skipping cooling gave 51 ± 2%. Cu loss helped explain the problem: about 84 ppm Cu appeared after unprotected cooling versus 19 ppm with protection, and about 13 ppm remained after polarization at −0.75 V versus RHE. My calculations trace a ligand-assisted route out of the metal, while Pb exposure means the yield changes cannot all be assigned to Cu alone.

In this post

  1. The cell changed while it cooled
  2. Negative potential helps, up to a point
  3. Start with a Cu atom at a kink
  4. Add partners, loosen the metal
  5. The vacancy stays on the receipt
  6. A stable product still needs an accessible path
  7. From losing metal to moving hydrogen
3.9 ± 0.2%amine yield after unprotected cooling
84 ppm → 19 ppmCu after cooling, without and with protection, approximately
13 ppmCu at −0.75 V versus RHE, approximately

The cell changed while it cooled

The experiment was supposed to begin after the cell cooled. The chemistry had already started. After an 18-minute cooling period, the subsequent amine yield was only 3.9 ± 0.2%. Holding a protective cathodic potential during that interval improved it to 30 ± 2%. Leaving out the cooling interval gave 51 ± 2%.

That is a large consequence for a step that could otherwise disappear into the experimental setup paragraph. I wanted to understand what the reaction mixture was doing to the electrode while everyone waited for the temperature to settle.

The experimental collaborators were studying reductive amination with a Cu cathode and Pb anode separated by a Nafion N-324 membrane. The catholyte contained 2.4 M acetone and 2.9 M methylamine added to 0.5 M KH₂PO₄ solution. The initial phosphate solution had pH 8.3, but the final mixture had pH 12.9 at 10 °C. The final mixture is what the electrode experiences. The starting buffer does not get the last word.

Cu concentrations after cooling were approximately 84 ppm without protection and 19 ppm with protection. That gives direct evidence that metal was leaving the electrode during preparation. Cathodic protection helped, but it did not reduce the measured loss to zero.

This follows naturally from Part 1. Methylamine had already shown that it could change the Cu–water environment. Here the same nitrogen functionality can change the coordination of Cu itself. The consequence reaches beyond an electrical response: some of the electrode ends up in solution.

Negative potential helps, up to a point

A cathode is a reducing electrode, so dissolution can initially sound backwards. Generating a cationic dissolved product carries an electrochemical cost that becomes less favorable as the potential becomes more negative. But that is only part of the free-energy balance. Ligands can stabilize the dissolved metal enough to offset a substantial part of that cost.

Potential-controlled experiments made the question more precise. After 30 minutes in the acetone–methylamine mixture, dissolved Cu decreased as the applied potential moved from +0.25 toward −1.25 V versus RHE. Approximately 13 ppm Cu nevertheless remained at −0.75 V. The smallest measured loss occurred at −1.25 V.

Those observations fit a conditional form of cathodic protection. Negative polarization opposes the formation of the compared cationic products, while the chemical environment supplies another driving force. To explain stability, I have to specify the potential and the ligands around Cu.

The yield has another passenger

The cooling experiments also involved a Pb anode and a membrane previously exposed to Pb. Later work established that trace Pb can strongly promote amination. That matters when interpreting the striking yield changes at the start of this post.

The dissolved-Cu measurements establish Cu loss independently. Yield can depend both on the changing Cu surface and on the inventory of a mobile promoter. Assigning every percentage point of the yield difference to Cu dissolution would require simultaneous control of Pb. I keep the cooling result as motivation and evidence of cell-history sensitivity, rather than using yield as a direct meter for how much Cu dissolved.

This is also why the cell boundary matters. The anode, membrane, solution, and cathode can exchange chemically important material. A label on each electrode does not keep their chemistry in separate rooms.

Start with a Cu atom at a kink

For the calculations, I compared a stepped and kinked Cu(843) surface with a close-packed Cu(111) terrace. A kink atom has six metallic neighbors; a surface atom on the terrace has nine. That difference gives the ligand a different starting point for extracting an atom.

I used ammonia first as a compact model ligand, then methylamine and ethylamine to examine alkyl substitution. Ammonia simplifies the geometry without implying that the actual reactant has identical steric or electronic behavior.

Amine adsorption is stronger at the kink than at the terrace by approximately 0.5 eV, with a potential-dependent difference. Its nitrogen lone pair makes a specific contact with Cu. More negative polarization weakens this donor interaction over the modeled range. The surface state and the ligand therefore respond to the same electrode potential from the beginning of the pathway.

Without an amine, moving a kink atom onto the adjacent terrace as an adatom costs approximately 1 eV in the investigated potential range. With one ammonia attached, the cost falls to approximately 0.1–0.3 eV. The ligand stabilizes the atom as it loses metallic neighbors.

That is the first useful piece of the mechanism. A ligand can change the cost of making the surface precursor that later dissolves. Complexation in solution and extraction from the solid belong to one connected pathway.

The displacement also changes which geometries are accessible. An adatom is more exposed than the original kink atom, leaving room for additional nitrogen donors. Extraction at the edge exposes another kink-like site, allowing the local motif to recur rather than using up a single special atom once.

Add partners, loosen the metal

A second and third ammonia can further stabilize the extracted Cu atom. A four-ligand surface structure is possible too, although the remaining surface contacts constrain its geometry. Detachment gives the complex more room to adopt a solution-like arrangement.

Bond analysis supplies a useful electronic view. As Cu acquires more nitrogen partners, the summed bonding contribution between that Cu atom and the surface decreases. For the four-ligand kink-derived complex, the reported Cu–Cu −ICOHP contribution falls by approximately a factor of two relative to the low-ligand reference.

Cu–N contacts grow as the metallic contacts weaken. ICOHP helps describe that redistribution of bonding, but it is not a bond-dissociation energy or an independently calculated detachment barrier.

I considered several dissolved coordination numbers and oxidation states. Within the selected products, the linear two-ligand Cu(II) complex was most stable; three-ligand Cu(I) and four-ligand Cu(II) species were also competitive over portions of the potential range. These are candidate thermodynamic endpoints, not a measurement of which species dominates the experimental solution.

The approximate thresholds were −1.1 V for the two-ammonia Cu(II) product, −0.9 V for the three-ammonia Cu(I) product, and −0.8 V for the four-ammonia Cu(II) product, relative to the compared surface state at the modeled pH. Dissolution becomes more favorable on the more positive side of each threshold.

These values explain why negative potential can reduce dissolution without eliminating it throughout the experimental window. They are specific to the ligand chemical potential, product activity, pH, and surface references used. Changing those conditions changes the balance.

Deep dive: the 0.51 and 0.21 eV comparison

For an illustrative four-ligand sequence at −0.7 V, the most uphill surface intermediate requires approximately 0.51 eV relative to the energetic reference used in that profile. Letting the fourth ligand approach during detachment gives an intermediate-state requirement of approximately 0.21 eV. The order of coordination and detachment matters. Neither number is a calculated transition-state activation barrier, so the comparison does not determine a numerical rate ratio.

The vacancy stays on the receipt

The terrace offers a useful bookkeeping lesson. Removing an atom from a perfect Cu(111) surface leaves a vacancy. Keeping that vacancy in the model makes the extraction sequence strongly unfavorable, with a cost of order 1.5 eV for the relevant surface state.

If I instead supply the vacancy from a bulk Cu reservoir, the cost becomes much lower. Those calculations describe different atom balances. The bulk reservoir has supplied something valuable, and the model has to say so.

A vacancy-compensated terrace calculation isolates the cost of the missing atom. It does not establish that an atom can migrate into that vacancy immediately on the experimental time scale.

The compensated terrace pathway resembles the kink sequence, but the flatter surroundings leave less room for several amine ligands. The four-ligand surface precursor is less comfortable there. Its dissolved endpoint can still approach the kink-derived threshold when the net removed atom is referenced to bulk Cu.

On a real electrode, steps, edges, and defects may supply atoms, and transport between those sites brings its own kinetic requirements. The kink pathway is the clearest local extraction picture. The compensated terrace model is useful as a limiting thermodynamic comparison. Keeping both makes the role of morphology easier to see.

A stable product still needs an accessible path

The ligand substitution comparison prevents an overly tidy ending. Methylamine and ethylamine stabilize the compared dissolved complexes more strongly than ammonia does, consistent with their donor character. Yet making the initial ligand-capped adatom costs more with substitution.

Experiments at −0.25 V found less dissolved Cu with the substituted amines than with ammonia. That direction is consistent with constrained access to the surface precursor, even though the final dissolved complexes are stabilized more strongly.

This is why I separate endpoint stability from accessibility. A molecule can be a good partner for dissolved Cu and still have difficulty reaching the right geometry on a crowded metal surface. Steric and interfacial constraints enter before the system gets to enjoy the favorable endpoint.

The intermediate profiles support that explanation qualitatively. They do not contain all the transition states needed to predict dissolution rates or long-term metal loss. The missing kinetics are a specific next problem: how quickly can the ligands and Cu atom move through the proposed route under matched operating conditions?

From losing metal to moving hydrogen

The outcome here is a chemically specific route for Cu loss under cathodic conditions. Amines bind low-coordinate Cu, stabilize its displacement, and help replace metallic neighbors with ligand coordination. The electrode potential opposes some of that chemistry, but cannot be interpreted independently of it.

The progression from Part 1 is small at the molecular level and large at the experimental level. First methylamine rearranged water around Cu. Now it rearranges who binds Cu. The relevant interface can change its composition during preparation as well as during electrolysis.

A mobile metal-containing species need not always mean a failed electrode. In Part 3, trace Pb offers a candidate route for carrying hydrogen between Ag and an imine. Its usefulness depends on whether the species can react productively and regenerate. The question shifts from keeping every atom still to understanding where it goes and whether it comes back.

Where this was published

Origin of copper dissolution under electrocatalytic reduction conditions involving amines, Chemical Science 15, 14485–14496 (2024). This post follows thesis Chapter 4. I performed the calculations and drafted the manuscript; experimental collaborators performed the measurements. The Pb qualification connects to the 2024 impurity study discussed in Part 3.
entry.summary: Part 2, Dissolution: amines help Cu exchange metallic neighbors for nitrogen ligands, so negative polarization reduces metal loss without always eliminating it

entry.title: Capacitance before reduction
entry.content:
Acetone raises Cu double-layer capacitance; methylamine lowers it. Both are individually more polarizable than water, so I modeled the water around them as well. The frozen-geometry water references give about 7.4 µF cm⁻² with one explicit layer and about 4.2 µF cm⁻² for the three-layer snapshot average, compared with about 13.35 µF cm⁻² for continuum solvent alone. The solutes change how that whole assembly responds, before the study reaches the more cathodic conditions used for organic reduction.

In this post

  1. Two solutes, opposite signs
  2. First, give Cu some water
  3. Acetone changes the neighborhood
  4. Methylamine rearranges it
  5. A response is not a head count
  6. Before reduction, the interface has changed
7.4 µF cm⁻²one-layer water reference, approximately
4.2 µF cm⁻²three-layer frozen-snapshot average, approximately
−0.32 Vmeasured minimum versus RHE, approximately

Two solutes, opposite signs

The first puzzle was a sign problem. Add acetone to the electrolyte around Cu and the measured capacitance goes up. Add methylamine and it goes down. If I treated either solute as an isolated, more polarizable replacement for water, I would have expected the same direction. The experiment was already telling me that the neighbors mattered.

This is the quiet beginning of the series. Acetone and methylamine are reactants in reductive amination: they can form an imine, which is then reduced to an amine. Before asking how that reduction works, I wanted to understand what the individual reactants do to the reaction environment.

The experimental collaborators measured impedance on polished Cu in 0.01 M NaClO₄, adjusted to pH 12 with KOH. The potential window was −0.227 to −0.527 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, or RHE. The capacitance minimum lay near −0.32 V versus RHE. These conditions give a useful starting point near zero charge, before a large faradaic reaction dominates the measurement.

Capacitance describes how much additional charge an interface accommodates when the potential changes. At a molecular interface, the answer depends on more than how squishy one electron cloud is. Molecule positions, water orientations, packing, and the distance over which charge is screened all enter. My task was to find chemically plausible structures that explain the opposite signs.

First, give Cu some water

I started with water on Cu(111), completed by a dielectric continuum representing the surroundings. Explicit water lets me distinguish molecules pointing hydrogen toward the surface, H-down, from those pointing oxygen toward it, O-down. These are orientation classes. The molecules have not acquired permanent job titles.

The sampled one-layer structures give approximately 7.3–7.5 µF cm⁻², with an average near 7.4 µF cm⁻². The three-layer frozen-snapshot average is approximately 4.2 µF cm⁻². The continuum-only reference gives approximately 13.35 µF cm⁻². Adding water molecules explicitly actually lowers the calculated capacitance.

That sounds odd if more water is supposed to mean more bulk-like screening. The crucial detail is what the calculation allows to move. Molecular dynamics lets water explore local configurations. I then evaluate charging with the nuclei frozen in each sampled geometry. The electrons respond, but the water molecules cannot rotate and reorganize under every charging perturbation. A high-dielectric continuum includes a response those fixed nuclei cannot provide.

Thickness matters, and the model notices

The supporting layer series gives approximately 7.4, 5.2, 4.1, and 3.5 µF cm⁻² for one through four explicit layers, respectively, read from the supporting plot. The three-layer value in that series and the snapshot average above come from their respective comparisons; I keep their labels attached rather than treating them as one identical number.

The continued change from three to four layers is a useful warning. This is sensitivity to the construction of the explicit region, not proof that the model has converged to a unique bulk-electrolyte capacitance. More explicit layers mean a thicker region whose frozen molecular arrangement screens differently from the continuum.

The familiar capacitors-in-series picture helps: the reciprocal capacitance accumulates contributions from thickness divided by screening strength. A thin, weakly screening region can have a large influence. Real molecular layers have no obligation to come with neat boundaries or a uniform dielectric constant, so I use the picture to explain direction rather than assign each water layer a measured permittivity.

Acetone changes the neighborhood

With the water reference in place, I replaced one layer in the three-layer model with acetone, placing it close to Cu, in the middle, or near the outer boundary. This tests how position changes the response while keeping the overall modeling approach consistent.

All tested arrangements increase capacitance relative to the three-layer water reference. Acetone nearest Cu gives the largest increase, followed by the intermediate placement. That makes chemical sense: a change close to the stored electrode charge has a particularly direct influence on screening.

Acetone brings a polar carbonyl group and two methyl groups. Its reported isolated-molecule polarizability is near 7.9 Å³, compared with a value of order 1 Å³ for water. But the carbonyl contact and the space occupied by the methyl groups also change the neighboring water. I cannot add molecular polarizabilities like prices on a grocery receipt and expect the interfacial total.

One-layer mixtures provide an independent check on the direction. Acetone can approach through a roughly vertical carbonyl contact or lie more parallel to Cu, leaving different room for water. The tested arrangements still give greater capacitance and polarizability than their water-only reference. Agreement in sign across these different constructions is more persuasive than the exact magnitude from one chosen structure.

The sizes of the changes are instructive. A representative three-layer arrangement gives an approximately 21% capacitance increase but an approximately 200% polarizability increase. A representative one-layer arrangement gives approximately 11% and 16%, respectively. The quantities move in the same direction without following a universal proportionality. They describe different responses under different boundary conditions.

I also checked what the trajectories were actually doing. Acetone stayed in its initially assigned region during the sampled motion. The bottom, middle, and top models therefore describe different local arrangements; their existence does not establish how frequently each occurs in the experiment. The model explains what an arrangement would do if present.

Methylamine rearranges it

Methylamine is the more revealing test because it defeats the isolated-molecule argument. It is individually more polarizable than water, yet the experimental capacitance falls as its concentration increases near the minimum.

Its nitrogen has several options. The lone pair can coordinate Cu or accept a hydrogen bond; N–H groups can donate hydrogen bonds. Local proton transfer can form a methylammonium–hydroxide pair. These possibilities let methylamine change the surrounding water network in ways that differ from the tested acetone arrangements.

In the three-layer models, every tested methylamine configuration lowers calculated capacitance and polarizability relative to the water reference. The strongest decreases occur close to Cu. One-layer calculations retain the same direction, whether the molecule is directly N-bound to Cu or held near the surface by its water environment.

The water-orientation analysis supplies a structural clue. Acetone trajectories retain broadly balanced H-down and O-down populations. Methylamine produces a more persistent H-down bias, particularly in the unbound middle and bottom arrangements. The surrounding water is participating in the solute effect.

Some methylamine configurations also develop local ion pairs. That is chemically relevant, but I would not appoint one ion pair as the sole cause of the entire response. Proton transfer, orientation, packing, and Cu–water contacts change together. Directly Cu-bound methylamine also has its lone pair occupied differently from an unbound molecule. The shared decrease across these cases is more robust than a unique microscopic explanation.

The distinction between organizing and responding matters here. Nuclear rearrangement selects the local electronic environment. The later frozen-geometry calculation measures the electronic response of that environment. It does not directly measure slow water rotation under an applied field. The molecules have arranged the room before I test how its electrons respond.

A response is not a head count

A capacitance measurement can tell me the interface has changed without telling me exactly which structure it became. Several arrangements can produce the same sign. To infer their populations, I would need adequate sampling, consistent chemical potentials, and the free energies of exchanging molecules between environments.

The trajectory diagnostics help keep this straight. Bounded energy fluctuations support local sampling. Layer-averaged molecular heights show that the assigned regions remain recognizable. Neither demonstrates that every relevant solvent-exchange barrier has been crossed. A middle layer with overlapping height fluctuations is not, by itself, evidence that all molecules exchange layers freely.

Deep dive: what the experimental capacitance includes

The impedance response was fitted with a resistance and a constant phase element, rather than an ideal capacitor. Effective capacitance was obtained from the fitted resistance and characteristic semicircle frequency and normalized by geometric area. That quantity depends on the equivalent circuit and real-electrode heterogeneity. I compare experiment and frozen-configuration calculations first through their trends, without assuming their absolute values are identical observables.

The same restraint applies to formation energies. Optimizing a structure taken from a final snapshot characterizes an endpoint; it does not turn it into a trajectory-averaged free energy. More negative total formation energy after adding water also partly reflects having more molecules. Neither observation supplies the equilibrium water-layer population.

The direction of the solute effect survives the tested model choices. The exact microscopic population and full frequency-dependent response remain open. That is enough to support a collective interfacial explanation, while leaving a useful next task for sampling and experiment.

Before reduction, the interface has changed

What I take from this comparison is that reactants start doing chemistry before their intended reduction step. Acetone and methylamine reorganize contacts around Cu, and that changes the electrical response. The electrolyte is already helping define the interface on which the later reaction takes place.

It would be tempting to carry the capacitance trend straight into a prediction of amine yield. The thesis does not support that jump. Organic reduction uses more cathodic potentials and different reaction mixtures. A changed charging response does not establish a changed imine-hydrogenation barrier, and higher capacitance is not automatically better catalysis.

Methylamine does, however, leave a useful lead. Its nitrogen can interact with water and with Cu. In Part 2, I follow that same coordination chemistry into a less comfortable question: what happens when the amine helps a Cu atom leave?

Where this was published

Probing the Electric Double-Layer Capacitance to Understand the Reaction Environment in Conditions of Electrochemical Amination of Acetone, ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces 17, 4087–4097 (2025). This post follows thesis Chapter 3. I performed the calculations and computational analysis; experimental collaborators supplied the measurements.
entry.summary: Part 1, Capacitance: acetone and methylamine change Cu double-layer capacitance in opposite directions, and the surrounding water explains why molecular polarizability is not enough

entry.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

link.title: A summer of molecules, puddles, and batteries

entry.content:
For my internship I left my UCLA computational chemistry desk for a while and joined SES AI, a battery company, as an Applied Scientist intern. The problem was that today's AI is very good with pictures and text, while chemistry and batteries live in 3D geometry, in physical time, and in scales that connect, where a tiny change in one molecule shows up much later as a battery that lasts longer (or doesn't). So the work ended up as a grid rather than a straight line: three scales stacked on top of each other, each known through several kinds of data, with the same small method run at every level.

In this post

  1. The picture in one diagram
  2. The scale axis: molecule, electrolyte, cell
  3. The modality axis: many ways to know each layer
  4. The same loop at every layer
  5. How representations flow upward
  6. The three parts
  7. What this got us

The picture in one diagram

The official title I gave the work was “multiscale multimodal intelligence across molecules, electrolytes, and cells,” which is a mouthful, so here it is as one picture instead.

Read it in three directions. Up the rows is the scale axis: what the thing is. Across the columns is the modality axis: how we get to know it. And the loop on the right of every row is the method, the same four steps each time. The short sections below take one direction at a time.

The scale axis: molecule, electrolyte, cell

Each row is a layer, and each layer is made of the one below it: molecules make up electrolytes, and electrolytes go into cells.

Think of a battery like a city. The molecules are the people. The electrolyte is the crowd, the liquid the ions swim through, made of salt, solvents and additives. The cell is the whole city, with its traffic jams, heat waves and aging infrastructure. You can’t understand a city from one person’s ID card, and you can’t understand a crowd without watching it move, so the work split into three parts, one per layer, each building on the last.

The modality axis: many ways to know each layer

At every layer, no single kind of data tells the whole story, and the layers don’t even share the same kinds. Here is what each row of the diagram actually holds.

Molecule

  • Images and text: molecule drawings in real papers (hand-drawn ones too) and what the paper says about them
  • 1D/2D/3D structure: SMILES and fingerprints, atom graphs, 3D conformers
  • DFT and MD properties: energies, HOMO/LUMO, how readily it gets reduced; solvation, density, diffusion, transport

Electrolyte

  • Recipes: components, amounts and conditions like temperature
  • DFT clusters: the ion with one partner, or a solvent and an anion competing for it
  • MD trajectories: about 40,000 of them, 5,000 frames each, roughly 200 million frames
  • Conductivity data, including the public CALiSol dataset

Cell

  • Multiscale simulations: DFT, MD, interface reactions, kMC, P2D/SPMe and 3D temperature and stress fields
  • Experiments: a 252-formulation, additive-centered DOE
  • Design and test conditions: protocol, temperature, C-rate

None of this is text in the way a chatbot would like. That was the question I kept asking all internship: can AI understand not just pictures and text, but 3D geometry, physical time, and how the scales connect?

The same loop at every layer

Only when I laid the three parts side by side did I notice that every layer runs the same loop: gather the data, learn a representation, align the different views of the same thing, then hand it to a co-scientist that helps decide what to do next. Prediction sits on top of the aligned space at every layer.

  Data Representation Alignment Co-scientist / decision
Molecule paper figures read by VLMs, checked by VERDICT 1D/2D/3D vectors 2D ↔ 3D partners (InfoNCE), keyed by InChIKey multimodal database in MU and a Chrome extension
Electrolyte polarizable force field, ~40,000 MD movies recipe, snapshot and trajectory heads three-way contrastive, one 128-d latent electrolyte co-scientist
Cell 252-formulation DOE plus a simulation ladder stacked molecule, electrolyte and cell reps cross-scale links, conditions as the glue aging world model, cell co-scientist, decision API

One lesson also kept showing up at every layer: a pretty number on the training objective is not the same as the scientific goal. A preference model can score beautifully and still get molecules wrong. A force field can nail tiny clusters and still ruin the liquid. An alignment can match molecules perfectly and still say almost nothing about real batteries. So most of my summer went into the checks: agreement between independent readers, liquid simulations inside the fitting loop, calibration against real measurements.

How representations flow upward

The layers aren’t three separate projects, because what one layer learns becomes input to the next. Nothing from the lower rows gets thrown away.

Molecule vectors become ingredients

Part 1 turns every recognized molecule into vectors. In the electrolyte layer those vectors become ingredients on the recipe side: a formulation network takes one vector per molecule, plus mixing ratios, salt concentration and temperature, and predicts how the mixture behaves.

The electrolyte latent and molecules build the cell

Part 2 turns every electrolyte into 128 numbers in a shared latent space, learned from recipes, snapshots and trajectories. In Part 3 a cell is represented by stacking those pieces: the molecule representations for each component, the electrolyte latent for the mixture, and the cell’s own design and operating conditions on top. The cell co-scientist reads the same stack, with 396 molecular, 274 electrolyte and 105 cell features per record in its early version.

The three parts

Each part walks through one row of the diagram in detail, in the order the stuff itself is built.

Part 1: molecules

Atom is atom, bond is bond. Reading molecules off real paper figures (59.8% exact on 331 journal figures), VERDICT’s four readers that may abstain, a rotation-aware recognizer, and 1D/2D/3D vectors in a multimodal database.

Part 2: electrolytes

Teaching a puddle to dance. A polarizable force field for 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, PFF RSI learning from more than 50 failed versions out of 80, three heads over about 40,000 MD movies, and an electrolyte co-scientist.

Part 3: cells

From molecules to batteries. A six-rung simulation ladder around a 252-formulation DOE, scales held together by test conditions, an aging world model that learns the whole evolution step by step, and a cell co-scientist.

What this got us

I started from batteries and ended up with a method. Batteries were just where I happened to begin; the method should transfer to similar multiscale systems, the ones built as molecules, then mixtures, then devices, where the important structure lives in drawings, geometry and simulations rather than text, and where experiments are scarce but simulation is possible. It’s still a living method, and I keep adding pieces as the field moves. Grab a snack: Part 1 starts at the bottom row, with a molecule and a computer trying to figure out who it is.
entry.summary: Overview of a three-part series on my Applied Scientist internship at SES AI: molecules make up electrolytes, electrolytes go into batteries, and each part builds on the representations of the one before

entry.title: From molecules to batteries
entry.content:
The electrolyte formulations from Part 2 go into real cells here, and the question becomes the one a battery company actually cares about: if I change the recipe, what changes in the battery? Starting from 252 additive-centered formulations, I stacked the molecule and electrolyte representations from Parts 1 and 2 into a cell representation, built a ladder of multiscale simulations around the real recipes, aligned the scales, trained an aging world model that learns how a cell evolves instead of guessing one lifetime number, and wrapped it all in a cell co-scientist. The clearest finding was that test conditions are the glue between scales: removing them collapsed a key cross-scale link score from 0.327 to 0.066.

In this post

  1. Δrecipe → Δperformance
  2. A cell is a stack of representations
  3. Simulations around the real recipes, lined up
  4. An aging world model
  5. Checking against real cells
  6. A cell co-scientist
  7. What this got us
252additive-centered DOE formulations
3,331electrothermal simulations linked to DOE records
0.327 → 0.066MD-to-electrode link score without conditions
41world-model architectures compared
24targets supported by sim-to-real calibration

Δrecipe → Δperformance

My starting point was a real, specific problem: a design of experiments (DOE) of 252 cell formulations built around additives, and a lot of questions about it.

Change the recipe, watch the battery

Within each comparison the electrodes were held fixed and the additives changed, so any change in performance can be pinned on the recipe. The question is simple to say: change the recipe, and what changes in capacity retention, cycle life, resistance and rate? On my slides that’s cycling, storage, charging and rate.

Slow bakes, plenty of compute

It’s a bit like baking. Swap one ingredient and the cake might rise higher, or collapse, or taste fine today and go stale next month. The annoying part is that each real bake for a battery is slow and expensive, and there was no budget for repeated new rounds of experiments. Compute, on the other hand, was available. So the plan was to use compute to fill in around the real data, while real measurements stay the reference. Simulations get to advise; they don’t get to overrule.

A cell is a stack of representations

The idea that unlocked this part is that nothing from Parts 1 and 2 had to be thrown away. Both were, underneath the jokes, a lot of representation learning.

Reuse, don’t restart

Part 1 turned every molecule into vectors from its 1D, 2D and 3D views. Part 2 turned every electrolyte into 128 numbers in a shared latent space, learned from recipes, snapshots and trajectories. A battery cell can be represented by stacking those learned pieces: the molecule representations for each component, the electrolyte latent for the mixture, and the cell’s own design and operating conditions on top.

Scales stacking up into a cell, like Lego bricks that were secretly designed to fit together. The storyline of the series is that molecules make up electrolytes and electrolytes go into cells, and here the representations follow the same path.

Simulations around the real recipes, lined up

A stack of representations needs something to learn from, and 252 formulations is not a lot, so I spent about a month building a high-throughput ladder of high-fidelity simulations around the DOE itself: around its real recipes and its real test protocols, not around made-up chemistry. No single simulation covers everything from electrons to a whole cell heating up, so each rung hands something to the next.

Six rungs

Here are the six rungs, in the order on my slides.

1. DFT

Electrons and local chemistry: whether an additive can be reduced, who coordinates around the ion, and how much energy it takes for a molecule to decompose. That local chemistry is the starting point for the liquid.

2. MD

How molecules organize and move in the liquid: solvation, aggregation, diffusion and conductivity. This is the PFF from Part 2, back for an encore, and it supplies what arrives at the electrode.

3. Interface reactions

How molecules may change near the electrode, the battery’s busiest border crossing, where bonds break and form. I explored these with a learned force model, and the events it finds become the moves for the next rung.

4. kMC

Kinetic Monte Carlo thinks in states, events and rates, like a board game where each move happens with some probability per unit time, to ask what happens next over long times. On the slide, kMC sits inside the cell model, the next rung.

5. P2D / SPMe

The whole cell’s transport and reactions: voltage, capacity and aging. P2D resolves what happens through the electrode’s thickness and inside its particles; SPMe is its simpler, cheaper cousin for when you need many runs fast. Both treat the cell as one stack.

6. 3D fields

Temperature and stress varying across the cell. I ran 3,331 electrothermal simulations linked to DOE records, using the recorded protocols, with stated assumptions about geometry and thermal inputs.

Deep dive: what the kMC rung did and didn't show

When I compressed MD transport into 12 states, the model’s held-out transition NLL was 1.612 versus 2.273 for an independent-state baseline (lower is better). Full SEI growth was not validated, so I’m not claiming it.

Every calculation keeps its recipe, conditions, source and a fidelity label: measured, calculated or predicted. Mixing those up is how you end up trusting a simulation more than the experiment it was supposed to explain.

Lining up the scales

With simulations at every scale, the next step was to connect them, the same way Part 2 connected recipes, frames and motion. Each input got its own encoder, mapped into a shared 128-d space. Then I learned links between neighboring scales: DFT ↔ molecules, molecules ↔ formulations, formulations + conditions ↔ MD, MD + conditions ↔ cells, cells + conditions ↔ DOE, plus links for the interface. The loss was a multi-positive InfoNCE, a fancy way of saying “pull together everything that belongs to the same experiment, push apart everything that doesn’t,” along with predicting the next scale’s vector from the current one.

To keep myself honest I trained four versions, three seeds each: the full model, no conditions, shuffled pairs, and no extra linking loss. Two findings stood out.

Conditions are the glue. Temperature, C-rate and protocol are what connect the scales: removing them collapsed the MD-to-electrode link score from 0.327 to 0.066. Without knowing how a battery was tested, the scales stop recognizing each other. Correct pairs also scored much better than shuffled ones, so the links are real.

The second finding is that molecules don’t get you to a battery just via alignment. Matching a molecule’s identity across views could be strong while the links to the real DOE stayed weaker. Knowing exactly who someone is doesn’t tell you how they’ll do at their new job.

Property heads

On top of the shared space sit regression and classification heads for property prediction. With chemistry inputs only, the normalized error (MAE across DOE targets) fell from 0.3341 to 0.2849 using modality dropout, which means randomly hiding inputs during training so the model learns to cope when some are missing. It cost a little when every input was available (0.2442 → 0.2542), a trade I’ll happily take. And the uncertainty was overconfident: nominal 90% intervals covered only about 68–78%. When the model said “I’m 90% sure,” it should have said “eh, maybe 70%.” Good to know, and now it’s written down.

An aging world model

The heads still predict a target as one number, and that’s the habit this section breaks: the goal shifted from predicting lifetime to learning the whole evolution process, how the cell’s state evolves under its design and its conditions.

From one number to the whole story

The usual black box takes the recipe in and gives one number out (“lifetime: N cycles”). It gives you nothing to check along the way, and when it’s wrong, it can’t tell you why.

Simulations as the practice data

To learn a process you need to watch it happen many times, and real experiments are few and slow. Simulations, on the other hand, give dense, state-by-state trajectories under many designs and conditions. So I ran a large number of P2D and 3D aging simulations: expensive, long DFN (full P2D) runs for some cases and cheaper, short SPMe runs for many more, screening early and recording why each run stopped. The 3D layer added 100,000 electrothermal entries and 200,000 chemical-mechanical results. The DOE stays the real-cell reference throughout.

How it works

Aging world model

Given the cell’s design, its current state (voltage, capacity, temperature, aging variables, state of health) and the condition (how it’s being used: protocol, temperature, C-rate), it predicts the next state. Then it rolls out: each prediction becomes the next input, step by step, into a full aging curve, and the lifetime is read off where the curve hits an endpoint, for example 80% of initial capacity. The same machinery covers calendar aging (sitting on a shelf) and cycle aging (being used).

It’s like predicting tomorrow’s weather, then using that forecast to predict the day after.

I compared 41 architectures on an early dataset of 6,258 simulated sequences × 140 steps, and the learned world model beat a direct MLP baseline on simulated sequences. My historical summary recorded roughly 24–27% lower error. I haven’t yet traced every one of those numbers back to its fold and target, and to be very clear, it is a lower prediction error on simulations, not an increase in anyone’s real cycle life.

Four checks

Next-step accuracy

Does one step forward land in the right place?

Long-run drift

Harsh, because each output becomes the next input and small errors snowball.

Direction of change

Does the curve move the right way when you swap an additive or a condition?

Agreement with experiments

Does it match real cells, not just the simulator?

The honest gap is that a model that learns the simulator very well can also inherit the simulator’s mistakes. How well it learns the simulations and how well it matches real cells are separate questions.

Knowledge emergence, carefully

Here’s the part that got me most excited, and I want to be careful with it. Because the model learns the process instead of memorizing endpoints, I started to see it pick up physically sensible chemistry and battery behavior that nobody spelled out for it, which is what I’d call knowledge emergence.

That’s my observation and interpretation, not a measured result. What I can point to is how it gets checked: rollouts are inspected for unphysical behavior in capacity, temperature and concentration at different horizons, held-out operating conditions test whether the model responds in the right direction, and the direction-of-change check is one of the four tests above. I’m not claiming it discovered anything specific like SEI growth or lithium plating. Confirming emergence rigorously is ongoing work, and probably my favorite open question from the summer.

Checking against real cells

Simulations are the practice field, not the match, so the last scientific step was to hold the models up against the DOE.

The VC plot twist

My favorite plot twist came from one additive, VC. In matched DOE comparisons it hurt cycle life in one cell design and helped in another. Same ingredient, opposite story. A physics model built on a fixed VC-SEI hypothesis reproduced some of the sign changes, but not the full direction and size of the effect. That sounds like a failure, but it’s the most useful kind of result: it turns the hypothesis into a candidate mechanism with a concrete next test.

Calibration, not self-grading

A rule I try hard to follow: don’t tune a model on the DOE and then hold up the same DOE as validation. That’s grading your own homework with the answer key taped to the back.

The bridge between simulation and reality is calibration against real experiments, and the sim-to-real calibration supported 24 targets. Everything else stays labeled for what it is: simulated until a real cell says otherwise.

A cell co-scientist

The last piece was the same move as at the end of Part 2, one scale up: hand everything to a co-scientist that can reason over it. This time the inputs come from every level.

Inputs from every level

In the early version, each record carried numbers from all three parts, 775 in all.

396 molecular

Molecular features from Part 1.

274 electrolyte

Electrolyte features from Part 2.

105 cell

Cell features from this part.

Each group goes through its own small projector into 4 “soft tokens,” and the 12 soft prefix tokens sit in front of the text, with missing inputs masked. Tokenization is chemistry-aware: common molecule names are kept as single tokens, with markers for chemistry and scale, so names get read as chemistry rather than letter soup.

Deep dive: text evidence, explanation examples and the training split

Next to the numbers goes text evidence: the recipe, the conditions, measured and simulated results, and where each came from. I also built explanation examples from evidence packages: a teacher model writes the explanation, and a critic plus fixed rules check it. A first pilot had 300 examples covering complete, missing, novel and conflicting evidence. On top of that come the data, the simulation logs and the tool-usage records. Held-out experimental answers stayed out of training, forward prediction can’t see the target value, and the split is by recipe. The fine-tuning itself is LoRA (QLoRA) on the LLM, trained together with the scientific projectors.

The harness and the split between two models

Cell co-scientist

The harness is DeepSeek Harness, connected to battery tools: cell prediction, recipe suggestions, similar experiments, cross-scale explanations, multiscale evidence, and formulation comparison, plus a call to the trained specialist that attaches the record’s evidence chain. A workspace keeps the conversation, the explanations and the tool history.

The work is split between two models: a larger LLM handles planning and tool calls, and the fine-tuned compact open-weight LLM acts as the scientific specialist. Its training data didn’t include tool-call trajectories, and I learned that good scientific answers don’t automatically give you reliable tool use.

What it can do

It connects recipes, conditions, simulated states and measurements; explains an answer with sources; compares candidate formulations; suggests recipes; finds similar experiments; and says what evidence is missing and what the next useful calculation would be. The interface shows the explanation, the tool calls, the returned results and the record IDs, and it marks every piece of evidence as measured, computed, predicted, missing or rejected. If you’ve read this far, you know why that matters to me.

To be honest about where it stands: in the demo, prediction and inverse design still used DOE retrieval and ranking of measured recipes, and connecting the world model is further work. A first explanation-training pilot didn’t improve the combined score, so it stayed experimental. And the reasoning text it writes is an output to inspect, not proof of what happened inside the model.

A decision API for the small judgments

Watching the agent work gave me one more idea, which is design thinking rather than a measured result. A lot of what an agent does all day is small and repetitive: is this record relevant, which of these four candidates fits, how complete is this evidence on a five-level scale. Those steps need judgment or a score, not long reasoning, and they’re exactly where a general LLM can wander off and return something malformed.

Jev decision API

I’d route those steps through a decision API to Jev, TypeSafe AI’s decision model, released on 15 September 2026 as a “System One” decision model. Jev answers typed questions about a text or JSON state and only returns structured outputs: a Choice (pick from up to 255 options, with probabilities), a Score (a position on a rubric of 2 to 10 levels that you describe), or a yes/no probability.

An independent evaluation reports 95–99% accuracy on several classification benchmarks and well-calibrated choice probabilities. Its “can’t hallucinate” guarantee is about format: the output always matches the declared schema, so no invented options and no parse errors. It isn’t a guarantee of correctness, and it can still pick a valid but wrong answer, which is why those steps still get checked. The point of the split is that the small judgments never come back malformed and come with calibrated probabilities, and the reasoning LLM is freed to do what it’s good at, which should make the whole agent stronger.

I’d like to say this is now a finished method of my own: represent, align, predict, then a co-scientist with a decision API. Honestly, the field moves so fast that I spent the summer chasing the frontier and bolting new pieces on, and I expect to keep doing that. It’s a living method, and this is its current version.

What this got us

The summer followed the stuff itself. Molecules got recognized and represented (Part 1), mixed into electrolytes whose rulebook, movies and latent space I built (Part 2), and went into cells, where the representations stacked up, the scales got aligned, a world model learned how the whole thing ages, and a co-scientist learned to reason over all of it (Part 3). Looking back, the same pattern showed up at every scale: represent, align, predict, and hand it to a co-scientist.

I started from batteries and ended up with a method. Batteries were just where I happened to begin, and I think the pieces add up to a framework that should transfer to similar systems: complex material and chemical systems built as molecules, then mixtures or formulations, then devices, where the structure lives in non-text data like drawings, geometry, trajectories and simulations, the scales are linked by conditions, and experiments are scarce but simulation is possible. Through all of it, real experiments stayed the reference: simulations explore, models propose, measurements decide. Now if you’ll excuse me, I have a mechanism test to think about.
entry.summary: Part 3, cells: the electrolyte formulations from Part 2 go into real batteries, and the molecule and electrolyte representations from Parts 1 and 2 stack up into a representation of the cell. Multiscale simulations around a 252-formulation experiment, alignment between scales, an aging world model that learns how a cell evolves instead of guessing one lifetime number, and a cell co-scientist that closes the series

entry.title: Teaching a puddle to dance
entry.content:
In Part 1 molecules got recognized and turned into vectors; here they get mixed into electrolytes, and the question becomes how they move. I extended a polarizable force field to 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, turned the failures of more than 50 of 80 versions into a self-improving fitting loop, and taught a model to read about 40,000 molecular-dynamics movies through three heads and one shared 128-number space. That space predicts conductivity with R² 0.976, and everything I learned along the way became training material for an electrolyte co-scientist.

In this post

  1. How do molecules move in a liquid?
  2. Writing a bigger rulebook
  3. The liquid gets a vote
  4. PFF RSI: turning failures into checks
  5. 40,000 movies and three heads
  6. The electrolyte co-scientist
  7. What this got us
627+molecules and 20+ anions in the force field
50+ of 80force-field versions failed in the liquid
~40,000MD trajectories, roughly 200 million frames
R² 0.976conductivity from the shared 128-d space
18 of 21held-out chemistry groups improved by trajectory features

How do molecules move in a liquid?

The question on my slides for this part was “how do molecules move in their micro-environment?”, and it starts with what an electrolyte actually is.

A crowded dance floor

An electrolyte is the liquid inside a battery that ions swim through. The recipe is simple: salt + solvents + additives, and those are exactly the molecules from Part 1, now with jobs. The behavior is not simple. Zoom in and it’s a crowded dance floor: lithium ions grab solvent molecules as partners, anions try to cut in, and how fast everyone gets across the floor decides how well the battery charges and discharges.

A rulebook and a movie

To watch that dance on a computer you need two things. A force field is the rulebook for how atoms push and pull on each other. Molecular dynamics (MD) is playing the movie with that rulebook: put lots of molecules in a box, apply the rules, and watch. If the rulebook is wrong, the movie is fiction. Very confident, beautifully rendered fiction.

Writing a bigger rulebook

My first job was to grow the rulebook so that the molecules people actually want to try have rules to follow. The force field is polarizable (PFF), meaning electron clouds can squish in response to their neighbors, which matters a lot around small, charged ions like lithium. The goal was coverage: extend it to 627+ molecules and 20+ anions, for both lithium and sodium electrolytes.

Reference data from quantum chemistry

The reference data comes from quantum chemistry (DFT), and lots of it. Some clusters are binary: the ion with one partner. Some are ternary: a solvent and an anion competing for the same ion, like two people reaching for the last slice of pizza. Each pair or trio gets computed at many distances and orientations, so the rulebook sees close calls, near misses and awkward side-on approaches, not just the polite pose.

What actually got fit

What I fit was mainly the exp-6 cross terms, keeping the charges and the polarization background fixed. All the while I was debugging, learning electrolyte science on the fly, and studying the properties that came out. Three jobs at once, which is roughly how every internship works.

Deep dive: what exp-6 means

Exp-6 is the part of the rulebook that covers short-range repulsion (“personal space!”) and dispersion, the weak, sticky attraction between everything. The “exp” is an exponential wall that keeps atoms from overlapping; the “6” is a gentle pull that falls off with the sixth power of distance.

The liquid gets a vote

The hardest lesson of the summer was that a fit isn’t done when the cluster error is low; it’s done when the liquid behaves. Density, radial distribution functions (who stands next to whom), diffusion, conductivity and viscosity all have to come out sensible in MD. My ledger ended up indexing 80 distinct force-field versions, and more than 50 of them failed. Here are a few of my favorite ways to fail.

The penguin huddle

One fit looked great on the clusters. Errors low, curves lined up, very satisfying. Then I ran the liquid and it clumped: the ions huddled together like penguins in a blizzard. I traced it to one ether-oxygen interaction the fit had effectively broken. Restoring it cut the ion aggregation fraction from 0.811 to 0.282, and from 0.415 to 0.044 in a second system. Conductivity moved closer to experiment, though it was still too low. Progress, not victory.

The wall that rounded to zero

A tiny coefficient, 0.00170, got rounded to zero on its way into the simulation. The builder treated zero as “missing” and helpfully swapped a big repulsive wall for a small one, and MD failed. Now a check reads the final built parameters, not just the ones I meant to build.

The helium incident

Lone-pair virtual sites stored with the label “He” were passed to DFT as real helium atoms. That quietly affected 27 of 61 clusters. Nothing says summer internship like accidentally inventing noble-gas electrolyte chemistry. Now templates, masses and site types are checked before anything goes out.

The failure that was a success

A salt-free solvent control came out at a viscosity of about 2.1–2.4 mPa·s, which told me the solvent was fine and the problem lived in the salt model.

An electrolyte has many jobs, and a rulebook that only nails small clusters can still flunk all of them in the liquid. The lesson I now believe in my bones: a low DFT fitting error doesn’t protect the liquid, and MD validation is part of parameter development, not a final demo.

PFF RSI: turning failures into checks

Fifty-odd failures is a lot of pain, but it’s also a lot of data, so I distilled them into a recursive self-improvement system, PFF RSI.

PFF RSI

The slide version is a simple cycle: fit the force field, validate in MD, record the failures, refine the next fit. When a brand-new molecule shows up, the loop runs on its own: sample, fit, guard, check in MD, learn, repeat.

Four layers under the cycle

Underneath the cycle, the slide stacks four layers.

Memory

A saved failure: the system, the version, what changed, what I expected versus what I measured, and what it cost, stored so it can be searched later by conditions, bad parameters, symptoms and useful checks.

Context

Loading the relevant failures before a new fit.

Code harness

Turning a failure into an automatic check, a new procedure written as code, so the same mistake gets caught by a machine instead of by me at 11 pm.

Weights

The fitted parameters that the whole loop keeps refining.

A new molecule arrives

When a brand-new molecule shows up, the loop samples a small starting set of clusters and expands only the channels that failed, fits, and checks. Parameters that match a known failure pattern get intercepted and sent to MD for a look before anyone uses them, so the wall that rounded to zero and the helium incident can’t sneak through twice. The honest caveat is that a fixed-budget test proving this memory actually makes research faster is still on my to-do list. It feels faster. Feelings aren’t data.

40,000 movies and three heads {#40000-movies-and-three-heads}

Once the rulebook works you can make movies, lots of them, and then you hit a new problem: none of it is text. Each trajectory is 5,000 frames, one every 4 picoseconds, for 20 nanoseconds in total. I ended up with about 40,000 trajectories, roughly 200 million frames.

You can’t paste a trajectory into a chatbot and ask how it felt. It’s coordinates, boxes and time, and the interesting part (who solvates whom, how ions hop) is spread across thousands of frames. So I asked whether a model could learn what a liquid is by watching, and squeeze each one into something small enough to search, compare and predict with.

Three views of the same liquid

I looked at the same liquid through three views, each with its own encoder, or “head,” in the same order as my slides.

1. Recipe

What’s in the bottle: the components, their amounts, and conditions like temperature, turned into 128 numbers.

2. Snapshot

One frozen frame of 3D atoms. It’s my favorite, so it gets its own subsection below.

3. Trajectory

Motion over time: the 5,000 frames are split into 50 chunks of 100, so the model sees how things move, not just a pose.

All three are compressed into one shared 128-d latent space and trained with three-way contrastive alignment: views of the same liquid are pulled together, views of different liquids pushed apart. A recipe should find its own movie, and a snapshot should find its own recipe. That one space then does three jobs: retrieval, alignment between views, and property prediction.
